strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: transferring rich vision-language representations into a compact detector that supports few-shot personalization without requiring the teacher or text prompts at inference.

Object-level supervision is sensible for detection, and the combination of pointwise feature alignment, relational geometry preservation, a learned cross-architecture translator, and PCA compression is coherent and reasonably motivated.

The evaluation covers four personalization datasets, both 1-shot and 5-shot regimes, multiple competing distillation approaches, oracle experiments, component ablations, and qualitative examples. The strongest configuration reaches a reported average of 58.7 versus 53.8 for AuXFT and 48.6 for the YOLO baseline.

The results generally indicate that multimodal supervision is more useful than either visual or textual supervision alone, while the PCA study provides useful evidence that the teacher representation can be substantially compressed.
The appendix acknowledges meaningful limitations, including expensive teacher-side training and poor scalability of prototype classification to many personal instances.
weaknesses: The construction of the central teacher target is technically unclear and appears inconsistent with LLaVA. The paper states that LLaVA-1.5-7B uses CLIP ViT-B/32, although the standard model uses a different vision encoder; it also applies the visual projector WT to a textual query, which is not how LLaVA embeds text. Section 3.2 describes an image-and-query-conditioned LLM representation, whereas Algorithm A.1 computes hi=fT(ci), apparently ignoring the image and the stated prompt. These discrepancies prevent reliable reproduction and leave unclear what information is actually distilled.

The evidence does not cleanly separate genuine multimodal fusion from concatenating CLIP features with class-label information. A label-only or otherwise controlled language baseline is needed, particularly because ground-truth class names are supplied to the teacher. The inconsistent definition of hi further complicates interpretation of the claimed multimodal benefit.

The strongest MOCHA result is initialized from the prior AuXFT method, making part of the gain cumulative. Although a COCO-initialized variant is reported, pretraining and distillation data differ across configurations and the baseline initialization is not described consistently enough to establish a fully controlled comparison. Averaging mAP and retrieval accuracy into one headline score also obscures task-specific effects.

Claims of lightweight, real-time, mobile, and minimal-overhead inference are unsupported by measurements. The paper reports training hardware and duration but provides no student/translator parameter counts, FLOPs, latency, memory, energy use, or comparison with AuXFT on deployment hardware.

The claimed architecture-agnostic nature is evaluated only with YOLOv8n and one teacher family. Core ablations are limited to PerSeg and iCubWorld, and there is no comprehensive matched experiment isolating the effects of the translator, relational loss, multimodal target, and initialization across all datasets.

Important reproducibility details are absent, including exact LLaVA checkpoint and feature layer, prompt/token construction, token pooling, PCA fitting protocol, batch composition for the pairwise loss, optimizer settings, learning rates, lambda values, temperature, episode counts, and random-seed protocol. Equation 3 also indexes normalization through d even though the PCA output has dimension dt.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently documented: the Wilcoxon tests omit sample sizes and the unit of analysis, do not address dependence among reused few-shot episodes, cover only two datasets, and produce nearly identical extremely small p-values. Thus they do not by themselves establish robust significance.

The manuscript contains unresolved cross-references such as “Tables ??” and “Figures ??,” and the pseudocode omits PCA/normalization and loss weights while contradicting the main method description. These are more consequential than cosmetic errors because they affect the specification of the algorithm.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: transferring rich foundation-model representations into a lightweight detector for few-shot personalized object recognition without requiring the teacher at deployment.
The object-level distillation pipeline is intuitive, combining region-pooled multiscale student features, a learned translator, pointwise alignment, and relational alignment.

Evaluation covers four personalization datasets and both oracle and end-to-end settings. The reported results generally improve over the undistilled YOLO baseline, with the strongest configuration averaging 58.7 versus 53.8 for AuXFT in Table 2.
The manuscript includes useful component analyses, PCA studies, qualitative examples, statistical testing, pseudocode, computational-resource information, and an explicit limitations section.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the technical novelty is limited. Region-level feature distillation, a projection/translation module, PCA compression, prototype classification, and pairwise relational knowledge distillation are established ingredients. The paper does not convincingly isolate what is fundamentally new beyond adapting and combining these components with AuXFT.

The strongest result is obtained by initializing from AuXFT and then comparing against AuXFT. This makes the claimed state-of-the-art gain difficult to interpret without an exact controlled baseline using the same initialization, training schedule, translator capacity, and additional compute but excluding only the proposed multimodal targets and relational loss. Table 3 does not supply this decisive control.

The evidence for the central multimodal claim is weak. In Table 2, visual-only and text-only MOCHA average 54.6 and 54.0, while the combined COCO-initialized model reaches 56.0. The much larger 58.7 result also changes initialization to AuXFT, confounding multimodal supervision with prior training. No statistical comparison isolates the improvement of combined visual-language supervision over the strongest unimodal alternative.

Important aspects of the teacher formulation appear technically inconsistent. LLaVA-1.5-7B is described as using CLIP ViT-B/32, whereas the standard model uses a different CLIP vision tower. The text also applies the vision projection matrix to a textual query and describes image-conditioned language-model features, while Algorithm A.1 instead computes hi=fT(ci), apparently without the cropped image. These descriptions do not define one reproducible teacher embedding pipeline.

Several mathematical details are erroneous or underspecified. Equation 3 indexes a dt-dimensional PCA vector over c=1,...,d; gamma=||hi|| does not by itself normalize the visual feature to the textual feature without accounting for ||zV,i||; and the relational softmax is not stated to mask self-distances before normalization, although the loss later excludes diagonal terms. These issues could materially change training.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently documented: dataset splits, numbers of personal classes and episodes, support/query sampling, confidence thresholds, handling of detection failures, random seeds, and the meaning of the reported standard deviations are absent. Hyperparameters including loss weights, temperature, optimizer settings, learning rates, batch size, translator architecture, and PCA fitting details are also missing.

The appendix reports extremely small Wilcoxon p-values, often around 1e-18, without sample sizes, test units, effect sizes, multiplicity correction, or justification that episodes are independent. It also says the tests use experiments from Table 1 even though the compared methods correspond to Table 2. The significance claim is therefore not reliable and may reflect pseudoreplication.

The headline average and the claimed +10.1 improvement combine heterogeneous quantities—detection mAP and retrieval accuracy—from unequal numbers of settings per dataset. This aggregate is not a well-defined vision metric and can obscure regressions; for example, the final model is worse than MSE+KL on iCubWorld 5-shot.

Claims of architecture agnosticism, minimal inference overhead, suitability for resource-constrained deployment, and performance on par with larger multimodal models are not adequately supported. Only one student and one teacher are tested, no parameter/FLOP/memory/latency measurements are given, the translator and prototype search remain active at inference, and no direct end-to-end comparison with a large multimodal detector is reported.

Baseline fairness is unclear. Methods designed for different tasks, such as ViLD, OFA, and generic KL/MSE distillation, are adapted without enough implementation detail or tuning evidence. The paper also lacks comparisons with broader recent personalized/open-vocabulary detection approaches and stronger compact students.

The ablations are incomplete and occasionally contradict the narrative: there is no full factorial separation of PCA, translator, pointwise loss, relational loss, multimodal target, and initialization; the relational-loss ablation changes only a few reported settings and yields mixed/small differences; and translator capacity is not controlled against parameter-matched MLP alternatives.

Presentation and attribution need substantial correction. Cross-references remain unresolved ('Tables ??' and 'Figures ??'), the related-work discussion incorrectly frames citations such as LLaVA, Transformers, and BERT as early personalization work, and phrases such as 'without loss of generality/generalization' are used where a specific implementation choice is being made. Collectively, the methodological ambiguity and confounded empirical evidence prevent a convincing acceptance case despite promising preliminary results.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important computer-vision problem: transferring rich vision-language representations into a compact detector for few-shot, instance-level personalization without requiring the large teacher or text prompts at deployment.

MOCHA is conceptually coherent. Region-level teacher targets, a cross-architecture translation module, pointwise feature matching, and relational geometry preservation form a sensible and reasonably original combination tailored to personalized detection.

The empirical results are consistently favorable across PerSeg, POD, CORe50, and iCubWorld. The strongest configuration raises the reported seven-column average from 48.6 for YOLO to 58.7 and outperforms the reported AuXFT baseline by 4.9 points. Even the COCO-initialized variant reaches 56.0, suggesting that the improvement is not entirely attributable to AuXFT initialization.

The paper evaluates visual-only, language-only, and combined supervision; compares against several distillation and open-vocabulary baselines; reports uncertainty; and includes component, dimensionality, initialization, and statistical analyses. The oracle experiment usefully separates representation quality from detection errors.

The inference-time design is attractive for resource-constrained applications: the large VLM is confined to offline distillation, while personalization uses frozen student features and a prototype classifier.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually well organized, with helpful system diagrams, pseudocode, qualitative examples, implementation-resource information, and an explicit limitations discussion. weaknesses: The description of the teacher is technically inconsistent and presently prevents confident reproduction. The paper states that LLaVA-1.5-7B uses CLIP ViT-B/32, although the standard LLaVA-1.5 configuration uses a different CLIP backbone. It also says that both visual and textual inputs are projected by the same visual projection matrix, while Algorithm A.1 reduces the language feature to h_i=f_T(c_i), contradicting the main text's claim that h_i jointly depends on the cropped image, class label, and prompt. The exact layer, token sequence, pooling operation, prompt, and image-text interaction need unambiguous specification.

The strongest headline comparison is not fully controlled: MOCHA(AuXFT) begins from the competing AuXFT checkpoint and then receives additional distillation, so its 4.9-point advantage over AuXFT combines the proposed method with extra training and compute. The same-initialization MOCHA(COCO) comparison remains positive but gives a smaller 2.2-point average gain. A matched-training-budget comparison would make the central claim more convincing.

The claimed benefit of multimodal semantics is only partially isolated. Teacher targets are conditioned on ground-truth class labels and a detailed descriptive prompt, so improvements could arise from extra label-conditioned supervision rather than genuinely grounded vision-language fusion. Comparisons against stronger class-label/text embeddings and image-independent prompted targets, plus a controlled visual-teacher baseline of comparable scale, would clarify the source of the gain.

The paper claims minimal inference overhead and suitability for real-time or mobile deployment, but reports no student parameter count, translator size, FLOPs, memory, latency, energy use, or device-level measurements. Because the translator remains active during inference, deployment efficiency is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Results average mAP50-95 and retrieval accuracy across datasets into a single headline score. These metrics have different meanings and scales, making the average difficult to interpret. Per-dataset improvements are more defensible, and significance testing should clearly specify the number and independence of episodes, the paired observation unit, and any multiple-comparison correction; the extremely small reported p-values otherwise provide limited reassurance.

Several presentation and methodological details require correction: Eq. 3 indexes channels to d although the PCA output has dimension d_t; the appendix contains unresolved references such as Tables/Figures '??'; the PCA discussion sometimes says 128-256 dimensions are optimal while the selected value is 512 and Tables A.5-A.7 often favor 256 or 384; and the relational-loss softmax normalization axis and treatment of diagonal entries are not precisely defined.

The evaluation is restricted to one student family, one principal teacher, and four relatively specialized personalization datasets. Broader students, teacher variants, and tests with many personal categories would better support the architecture-agnostic and real-world scalability claims, especially given the authors' acknowledgment that prototype matching scales poorly.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: transferring rich vision-language representations into compact detectors for few-shot, instance-level personalization without requiring the teacher or text prompts at inference.

The region-level distillation framework is intuitive, combining pointwise feature matching with relational geometry preservation. The visual, textual, and combined-supervision comparisons provide some evidence that the modalities are complementary.

The empirical evaluation covers four personalization datasets, multiple student architectures, several few-shot classifiers, component ablations, computational measurements, and both 1-shot and 5-shot settings. MOCHA reports consistent gains, including an average increase from 48.6 to 58.7 over the YOLOv8n baseline and from 53.8 to 58.7 over AuXFT.

The absolute deployment footprint remains moderate, and caching teacher embeddings is a practical way to avoid repeatedly running the 7B teacher. The appendix includes pseudocode, hardware details, per-dataset results, and an explicit limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The teacher formulation appears technically inaccurate or, at minimum, too ambiguous to reproduce. LLaVA-1.5 does not normally embed textual queries through the visual projection matrix as stated, and the claimed CLIP ViT-B/32 visual encoder is inconsistent with the standard LLaVA-1.5 configuration. The pseudocode further defines h_i=f_T(c_i), omitting the crop-conditioned visual-language interaction and prompt described in the main text. These discrepancies concern the central source of supervision rather than a cosmetic detail.

The strongest result, MOCHA (AuXFT), starts from an AuXFT-pretrained model and then receives another 20 epochs of training on OpenImages plus a larger translator. There is no matched control that gives AuXFT the same additional detection training, parameter capacity, and optimization budget without the proposed losses. Consequently, the reported +4.9 improvement over AuXFT cannot be cleanly attributed to MOCHA.

Several baseline adaptations are under-specified. In particular, it is unclear how output-space KL distillation from LLaVA, ViLD, and OFA are instantiated and tuned in this personalized-detection setting. Dataset sizes, class/split definitions, episode construction, number of trials, and key optimization hyperparameters are also missing, despite reliance on an external prior protocol. This substantially limits reproducibility and makes fairness difficult to verify.

The statistical evidence is not adequately documented. The Wilcoxon tests report extremely small p-values without sample counts, test statistics, independence assumptions, or correction for multiple comparisons. Episodic evaluations often share images and support examples, so treating all episode scores as independent can greatly overstate significance.

The headline average combines mAP on PerSeg/POD with retrieval accuracy on CORe50/iCubWorld. Although arithmetically valid, averaging heterogeneous metrics makes the claimed +10.1 improvement difficult to interpret. Results should be summarized per metric/task family, and full detection evaluation should more clearly separate localization, proposal recall, and personalized classification.

The efficiency discussion is internally inconsistent. The main text claims a 3 ms overhead over YOLOv8n, whereas Table 6 reports MOCHA at 35.2 ms and the baseline at 50.5 ms, making MOCHA unexpectedly faster. Moreover, parameters increase from 3.2M to 4.5M, VRAM from 221.5 to 352.5 MB, and model size from 12.2 to 22.8 MB; these nontrivial relative increases weaken the broad claim of minimal inference cost. Teacher-feature preprocessing time and storage are not clearly included.

Important methodological details remain ambiguous: the axis used for each softmax in the relational loss, the definition of normalized Euclidean distance, whether relational pairs span an image or an entire batch, the exact ROI-feature extraction procedure, and how PCA/normalization are applied during training. The scaling gamma=||h_i|| only equalizes modality norms if the visual feature is already unit-normalized, which is not stated.

The relational-loss ablation shows only modest and inconsistent gains, while the illustrative 2D-to-3D toy experiment does not establish its value in detection. A matched L_dist-only study across all four datasets, confidence intervals for paired improvements, and a stronger control for extra training are needed to support the claimed technical contribution.

strengths: As an Algorithms/General contribution, the paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: transferring multimodal knowledge into a lightweight detector for few-shot instance personalization without requiring the large teacher or text input at inference.

The region-level distillation formulation is practically motivated, and combining direct feature alignment with relational alignment is reasonable. The prototype-based personalization stage also permits inexpensive adaptation while keeping the detector frozen.

The empirical evaluation is broad: four personalization datasets, several distillation baselines, multiple student architectures, different few-shot classifiers, PCA studies, component ablations, qualitative examples, and computational measurements are included.

The reported improvements are substantial. The strongest configuration improves the stated aggregate from 48.6 to 58.7 over YOLOv8n and from 53.8 to 58.7 over AuXFT. The visual-only, text-only, and combined-feature results provide some evidence that the modalities are complementary.
The paper is generally readable, contains useful diagrams and pseudocode, and explicitly discusses limitations concerning training cost, task specificity, and scalability of prototype matching.
weaknesses: The teacher-feature construction is not described in a technically consistent or reproducible way. Section 3.2 says visual and textual inputs are jointly processed by LLaVA to produce an interaction-dependent sequence, whereas Algorithm 1 computes h_i=f_T(c_i), apparently from the class label alone. The stated projection H_Q=W_T Z_Q is also inconsistent with standard LLaVA, whose multimodal projector maps visual features into the language-model token space rather than projecting text tokens through the same matrix. The manuscript additionally identifies the LLaVA-1.5-7B visual encoder as CLIP ViT-B/32, which does not match the standard model configuration. Hidden layer, token selection, prompt/response handling, and averaging details are missing. These issues undermine both reproducibility and the claim that h_i is a fused region-language representation.

The relational objective is materially underspecified. It is unclear whether the softmax in Eq. 7 is row-wise or global, what “normalized Euclidean distance” means, and how temperature or batch size is handled. More importantly, the pseudocode computes the distance distribution among boxes within each image, despite claims of preserving global embedding geometry. Images with one or very few boxes provide no meaningful relational signal. The implementation scope must be clarified and ablated.

The headline comparison is not fully clean: MOCHA(AuXFT) starts from AuXFT-pretrained weights and is then compared against AuXFT itself, so the claimed +4.9 gain is partly an additional-training comparison rather than an independent alternative. The COCO-initialized MOCHA variant has a smaller aggregate advantage of 2.2 over AuXFT. Training schedules and compute are not controlled across methods, and the adaptations of ViLD, OFA, KL, and MSE+KL to this specialized protocol are insufficiently documented to establish fair reproduction.

The reported “Avg” mixes mAP50-95 on PerSeg/POD with retrieval accuracy on CORe50/iCubWorld and gives equal weight to seven heterogeneous dataset/shot columns. Consequently, the +10.1 and +4.9 headline improvements are not a well-defined single-task performance measure. Dataset sizes, split construction, episode counts, and sampling protocol are also not clearly reported, while PerSeg is evaluated only in the 1-shot condition.

The statistical analysis is not convincing. Nearly every Wilcoxon comparison produces essentially the same extraordinarily small p-value near 10^-18, but the number and independence of paired observations are omitted. Treating correlated few-shot episodes as independent would constitute pseudoreplication. There is also no multiple-comparison correction or effect-size analysis.

The edge-deployment claim is not adequately supported. All experiments use server GPUs, with no latency, energy, or memory measurement on an actual mobile or robotic platform. Table 6 even reports the undistilled YOLO baseline as slower than both larger distilled systems, without explaining the measurement anomaly. Training-time descriptions also alternate between 11 and 28 hours depending on initialization, making the efficiency narrative easy to misread.

The core technical novelty appears incremental: concatenate pretrained visual and language-derived features, apply PCA/channel scaling, learn a translator, and add a pairwise-distance loss. The paper needs a more complete positioning against multimodal/open-vocabulary representation distillation and stronger evidence isolating what is specifically gained from LLaVA-generated semantics rather than additional supervision and training.

Several smaller inconsistencies reinforce the reproducibility concern: Eq. 3 indexes channels to d rather than the retained dimension d_t; the main text refers to Table 7 where the relevant table is Table 3; “global” alignment is not reflected in the supplied algorithm; and important hyperparameters such as loss weights, optimizer settings, batch size, prompt decoding configuration, and relational-loss normalization are absent from the manuscript. Overall, the empirical promise makes the decision close, but these technical and evaluation ambiguities currently favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: transferring rich vision-language representations into compact detectors for few-shot, instance-level personalization without requiring the teacher or text input at inference.

The proposed combination of region-level multimodal targets, a cross-architecture translator, pointwise feature matching, and relational geometry preservation is coherent. Although the individual ingredients are familiar, their integration for efficient personalized detection is useful and reasonably original.

The empirical results are strong and broad. MOCHA improves over the undistilled YOLOv8n baseline across four datasets and generally outperforms AuXFT, ViLD, OFA, and conventional output/feature-distillation alternatives. Experiments with YOLOv8n, several YOLOv11 variants, and RT-DETR provide evidence that the approach is not tied to one student architecture.

The paper includes useful analyses of visual versus linguistic supervision, PCA dimensionality, the relational loss, translator components, downstream few-shot classifiers, computational overhead, qualitative behavior, and statistical significance. The reported inference latency increase is modest, supporting the practical motivation.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful diagrams, pseudocode, implementation details, and an explicit limitations section.
weaknesses: The strongest headline comparison is not entirely clean: MOCHA (AuXFT), which achieves the reported 58.7 average and the stated +4.9 gain, starts from an AuXFT-pretrained checkpoint. The independently initialized MOCHA (COCO) reaches 56.0, only +2.2 over AuXFT. Thus, the best result demonstrates a useful refinement of AuXFT more clearly than a standalone replacement for it.

The efficiency comparison is potentially misleading. Table 6 assigns MOCHA (AuXFT) 11 training hours while apparently excluding the approximately 50 hours required to produce its AuXFT initialization. The claim of reducing complexity by several orders of magnitude is also not substantiated by the reported wall-clock reduction. End-to-end training cost and energy should be reported consistently for every initialization.

The description of LLaVA is technically imprecise and internally inconsistent. LLaVA-1.5 does not simply contain separate LLaMA visual/text encoders with one shared projection matrix applied to both image and text representations, and its standard visual encoder is not CLIP ViT-B/32 as stated. Moreover, the main text describes image-and-label-conditioned LLM features, whereas Algorithm 1 writes h_i=f_T(c_i), apparently omitting the image-conditioned interaction. Exact layer outputs, token aggregation, prompt construction, and LLaVA variant must be clarified for reproducibility.

Important evaluation details are underspecified, including dataset splits and conversions, class/sample counts, the number and construction of few-shot episodes, whether results share identical detector proposals, and the precise retrieval protocol. Averaging mAP and retrieval accuracy across heterogeneous datasets into one headline score is convenient but difficult to interpret.

The Wilcoxon analysis does not identify its independent experimental unit or number of trials. Extremely small and frequently identical p-values may reflect treating correlated episodes as independent samples; seed-level or subject/class-level tests and confidence intervals would provide more credible evidence.

The approach can only relabel boxes already proposed by the generic detector, so it cannot recover personalized objects missed by the base detection head or objects outside its proposal coverage. This materially narrows the deployment claim and deserves direct recall analysis. The on-device motivation is also supported only by measurements on an NVIDIA L40S rather than actual edge hardware.

Novelty is moderate: multimodal concatenation, PCA/whitening, feature translation, pointwise distillation, and pairwise relational matching are established components. Acceptance rests primarily on the effective system integration and empirical improvements rather than a fundamentally new learning principle.
